Senses.Explanation: To degrade a free person into servitude is to impose a lower status on someone who was not bound to it; Chan speakers use the legal-social wrong as a charge of falsely diminishing what is already present. Foyan Qingyuan calls excessive explanation 'degrading the free into servitude.' Tianyin Yuanxiu puts the charge into a reply to an elder and also denies that saying everyone possesses the matter is such degradation. Feiyin Tongrong explicitly says equating a bound being with Shakyamuni is neither degrading the free nor calling the base noble, while Yunmen Wenyan makes 'do not degrade the free' a stock counter before a blow. Huayan Shengke turns the same charge against treating Shakyamuni as awake and the assembly as not. These cases bend a status offence into an interview accusation: the named master says the proposed distinction or explanation has needlessly lowered its subject.

Senses.Explanation: The host within the guest names a guest–host position whose interpretation is explicitly system-dependent in later Chan analysis. In the later systematic account of Linji's four guest-host configurations, this is the configuration named when ‘the student has a nose-hole’ (學人有鼻孔). Records then raise the label as a public question and preserve different answers, including 'facing him, there is no companion.' This is one member of the fourfold set alongside host-within-host, guest-within-host, and guest-within-guest. The texts explicitly say that Linji's guest-host system differs from Caodong's, so the shared graphs must not blur the two school-specific things.

Senses.Note: Separate school-specific referent, not a competing reading of one saying. Variant answers are retained as deployments within the Caodong positional category and are not split further.

Senses.Explanation: This separate sense denotes Caodong host-within-guest position, not Linji host-within-guest configuration. In Caodong guest-host discourse the same words name a position paired with host-within-guest's converse and with the bent-and-upright vocabulary. The Eye of Humans and Gods explicitly glosses Caodong's host-within-guest as 'function within essence' (用中體) and says this fourfold guest-host system is not the same as Linji's. In the Dongshan encounter, Dongshan asks 'what is host within guest?' and receives 'white clouds cover the green mountain'; another transmitted version assigns 'long years not leaving the house.' Later verse can say 'host within guest is precisely guest within host' and tell the hearer not to recognize a fixed pattern in reversal and accord. These are recorded formulas and answers, not an invitation to supply an interpretation beyond them.

Senses.Explanation: Guest and host are the paired roles through which an encounter's initiative and response are described. Records ask whether the roles are distinguished, show one role questioning the other, and speak of their positions turning or being exchanged. Interchange does not name a second thing: it is an action performed with the same guest-host pair. The phrase can refer to literal social positions, but in encounter analysis it marks who sets and who receives the situation.

Senses.Explanation: Host and guest exchange roles when the initiative and responsive positions in an encounter can reverse without losing their distinction. Hongzhi Zhengjue says that Buddha and Caoshan exchange host and guest while each has an eye for appearance before and after emergence. Xuedou Chongxian says that an eye at the hundred-foot pole enables host and guest to exchange and enter the tiger's cave. Hanyue Fazang joins the exchange to whole-body taking and releasing by Linji's true descendants. In another raised encounter, Hongzhi calls Tianxian and Piyun's exchange clear in its entrances and exits. Together the cases support reversible encounter roles rather than a generic change of identities.

SearchAliases: the Han hound chases the clod
a Han hound pursuing a dirt clod
the Han-family hound runs after the clod
Zen Han hound chases the clod
Senses.Explanation: A Blue Cliff Record comment gives the named allusion: the hound of the Han family was a swift dog, capable of tracking the cunning hare of Zhongshan; Yuanwu Keqin compares the unnamed monk in Dongshan's cold-and-heat exchange to that hound running up the steps after a reflected moon and finding no moon there. Across the corpus the compact phrase is repeatedly contrasted with "the lion bites the person" (師子咬人，韓獹逐塊): one address says, "you must have the lion bite the person; do not imitate the Han hound chasing the clod" (直須師子咬人，莫學韓獹逐塊). It also occurs as a verdict after answers in public exchanges and as a verse line on Zhaozhou's attendant case. Zen bends the old hunting-dog allusion into a stock contrast between the person and the thrown clod, but the entry goes no farther than the corpus's own lion/person and hound/clod pairing.
